Hill-climb jointly over the column permutation and the 25 possible rotations per column (or note that the SAME keyword letter sets both rotation and order, so hill-climb over keyword strings of length C from a dictionary), scoring recovered rows with tetragram fitness. CryptoCrack treats it as a constrained double transposition and brute-forces/dictionary-searches the keyword.
notes: CRITICAL details: length must be a multiple of 25; 25 rows; W folded into V (25-letter alphabet); rotation amount derived from the REVERSED alphabet AZYX...CB (so A=0, B=24, ... Z=1). Column permutation is ordinary alphabetical-by-keyword. Read OUT by rows.

name: Swagman
algorithm: A transposition using an n x n KEY SQUARE that is a Latin square of the digits 1..n (no digit repeats in any row or column). ENCRYPT: (1) Choose square size n (ACA: 4..8, sometimes stated 3..7). Build an n x n key square filled with 1..n so no digit repeats in a row or column (a Latin square; derived from a numeric key). (2) Write the plaintext horizontally into a rectangle with exactly n rows, in blocks n columns wide (i.e. consecutive n x n blocks side by side), adding null letters to complete the final block/row. (3) Encipher each n x n plaintext block independently: for each COLUMN of the block, reorder its n letters VERTICALLY according to the corresponding column of the key square — the plaintext letter sitting in the row that holds key-digit 1 goes to ciphertext row 1, the letter in the row holding digit 2 goes to row 2, etc. (4) Read the ciphertext off VERTICALLY (column by column, block by block) in 5-letter groups. DECRYPT: With the same key square, invert the per-column permutation in each block: the ciphertext letter in row r goes back to the plaintext row that holds key-digit (r+1) in that key-square column. Then read the rectangle by rows to recover plaintext (strip nulls). Encrypt!=decrypt. No alphabet/I-J; period = n (square size).
key_format: A square size n (4..8) plus a numeric key defining an n x n Latin square (each row/column a permutation of 1..n). Given as the rows of the square, e.g. 5x5: 32145 / 15324 / 24531 / 53412 / 41253.

Letters never leave their column, only change rows within the block, so the i-th letter of every block-column stays in that column — a strong structural constraint for cracking.

name: Nihilist Transposition
algorithm: A double (columns-then-rows) keyed transposition on a square grid, SAME key applied to both columns and rows. Grid is n x n (ACA max 10x10); len must be a perfect square (pad if needed). ENCRYPT (Elcy / writing-in-key version): (1) Write plaintext into Square 1 by rows, n x n, with the key digits labeling BOTH the columns (across the top) and the rows (down the side). (2) Square 2: permute the COLUMNS so the column key-digits are in ascending order (move column labeled 1 to position 1, etc.). (3) Square 3: permute the ROWS of Square 2 so the row key-digits are in ascending order. (4) Take the ciphertext off Square 3 either BY COLUMNS or BY ROWS (a stated convention). DECRYPT: reverse — write the ciphertext into Square 3 by the same take-off route, restore original row order (inverse row permutation), restore original column order (inverse column permutation), then read Square 1 by rows. LEDGE / taking-out-key variant: the key is placed so that it labels the SORTED order (columns are permuted INTO numerical order, then rows into numerical order); writing-in and taking-out keys are inverses of each other, and for self-inverse keys (e.g. 2134) both methods give identical results. Encrypt!=decrypt in general. No alphabet/I-J.
key_format: One numeric key (a permutation of 1..n) used for BOTH the column permutation and the row permutation. CryptoCrack note: for 'The ACA & You' compatibility, nihilist keys are the inverse of columnar keys.

name: Nihilist Substitution
algorithm: SETUP: Build a 5x5 Polybius square from a keyword. Take the keyword, drop repeated letters, then append the remaining unused letters of the alphabet in order. J is merged into I (25-letter alphabet). Fill the square left-to-right, top-to-bottom. Label rows and columns 1..5. Each letter's value is a two-digit number = (row digit)(column digit), ROW FIRST. ENCRYPT: (1) Convert each plaintext letter to its two-digit square coordinate. (2) Take a SECOND keyword (the additive key), convert each of its letters to two-digit coordinates using the SAME square; this key sequence repeats cyclically to the length of the plaintext. (3) For each position, ciphertext number = plaintext number + key number (ordinary decimal addition, NOT digit-wise mod). Results range roughly 22..110; ACA convention leaves them as printed (often 2- or 3-digit). Some implementations reduce any sum >100 by subtracting 100 (keep last two digits). DECRYPT: subtract the repeating key number from each ciphertext number (add 100 first if the ciphertext digit pattern requires it), giving a two-digit number whose tens digit is the row and units digit is the column; look up the letter. Encrypt != decrypt. Note: because each plaintext/key coordinate digit is 1..5, a ciphertext two-digit group can be uniquely split (units in 2..10, tens in 2..10) which is how the adversary segments.
key_format: Two keywords: one builds the 5x5 square (mixed alphabet), one is the repeating numeric additive key (also enciphered via the same square). Period = length of the additive keyword.

name: Checkerboard
algorithm: SETUP: Build a 5x5 keysquare from a keyword (drop duplicates, append unused letters A-Z in order, J merged into I, 25 letters), filled row-wise. Choose TWO 5-letter keywords with no repeated letters: one labels the ROWS (down the left side), one labels the COLUMNS (across the top). ENCRYPT: locate each plaintext letter in the square; replace it by a DIGRAPH = (row-label letter)(column-label letter), ROW LETTER FIRST. Plaintext length L -> ciphertext length 2L. DECRYPT: take ciphertext in pairs; first letter selects the row (via the row keyword), second selects the column (via the column keyword); read the plaintext letter at that cell. Encrypt != decrypt. (Variant: if the cipher is set up with two row words and two column words, either of the paired key letters may stand for that coordinate, adding homophony; ACA standard uses one 5-letter word per axis.)
key_format: Three keywords: keysquare keyword + a 5-letter ROW keyword + a 5-letter COLUMN keyword (each axis word has 5 distinct letters).

crack_approach: Ciphertext uses only the 10 key-letters (5 row + 5 column) and always reads as digraphs alternating a row-letter then a column-letter, so identify the two 5-letter alphabets by position parity. Reduce to a 25-symbol monoalphabetic substitution on the digraphs and solve as an Aristocrat/Patristocrat with hill-climbing + n-gram (quadgram) fitness over the 5x5 keysquare; the two axis words fall out from the digraph alphabets.

name: Bazeries
algorithm: SETUP: (1) Choose a key NUMBER under 1,000,000. (2) LEFT square = the plain alphabet A-Z (J merged into I) written by COLUMNS into a 5x5 grid (i.e. read down columns: A F L Q V / B G M R W / ... per CryptoCrack's column-fill convention). (3) RIGHT square = a keyed alphabet derived from the key number SPELLED OUT in words: spell the number (e.g. 7352 -> SEVENTHOUSANDTHREEHUNDREDANDFIFTYTWO), drop repeated letters (-> SEVNTHOUADRFIYW), append unused alphabet letters in order (-> SEVNTHOUADRFIYWBCGJKLMPQXZ), J merged into I, filled by ROWS into the 5x5. ENCRYPT: (a) TRANSPOSE: divide plaintext into successive groups whose lengths cycle through the digits of the key number (e.g. 7352 -> groups of 7,3,5,2,7,3,5,2,...) and REVERSE the letters within each group. (b) SUBSTITUTE: for each (now transposed) letter, find it in the LEFT square and replace it with the letter at the SAME row/column position in the RIGHT square. DECRYPT: substitute right-square->left-square, then re-group by the same digit cycle and reverse each group again. Encrypt != decrypt.
key_format: A single integer key (1..999,999). It both seeds the keyed right-hand alphabet (spelled out) AND defines the cyclic group lengths for the reversal transposition.

test_vectors.plaintext: A CLEAR CONSCIENCE IS USUALLY THE SIGN OF A BAD MEMORY
test_vectors.ciphertext: RASMVRS YIG RIMCR CM VVSXYXY FKL IOCYM EG UMUBSHS LAG
test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Bazeries page. Intermediate (group-by-7,3,5,2 then reverse each group): 'craelca sno cneic ie llausus hty ngise fo memdaba yro'; keyed right alphabet SEVNTHOUADRFIYWBCGJKLMPQXZ.

crack_approach: Brute-force the key number 1..999,999: for each candidate, build the keyed right alphabet (from the spelled-out number) and the digit-cycle transposition, decrypt, and score with quadgram fitness; the spelling constrains plausible alphabets so simulated-annealing / dictionary attacks on the implied keyword plus a search over short transposition cycles also work.

name: Gromark
algorithm: Name = GRonsfeld + Mixed Alphabet + Running Key. SETUP: (1) Choose a 5-digit numeric PRIMER. (2) Build a running numeric key by LAGGED-FIBONACCI / chain addition: the next digit = (digit_i + digit_{i+1}) mod 10, generating digits left-to-right and appending, until the key is as long as the plaintext. (Primer 12345 -> 1+2=3,2+3=5,3+4=7,4+5=9,5+3=8,... giving 1 2 3 4 5 3 5 7 9 ...). (3) Build a MIXED (cipher) alphabet by columnar transposition (K2-type/'sequence transposition'): write the keyed keyword alphabet into a block whose width = keyword length, number the columns by the alphabetical order of the keyword letters, then read the block off column-by-column in that numeric order to get a 26-letter mixed alphabet. ENCRYPT: align the STRAIGHT plaintext alphabet A-Z (positions 0..25) above the MIXED alphabet. For each plaintext letter take its index i in the straight alphabet, add the running-key digit d (0..9): ciphertext letter = MIXED alphabet at position (i + d) mod 26. DECRYPT: find ciphertext letter's index j in the MIXED alphabet, plaintext = straight alphabet at (j - d) mod 26. The primer is transmitted as the first group; the last running-key digit is often appended as a check digit. Encrypt != decrypt.
key_format: A 5-digit primer + a keyword (for the mixed-alphabet columnar transposition). Period is effectively the full message (running key) until the chain sequence repeats (period of the 5-digit chain can be up to 10000).

test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Gromark page (worked example). Running key = 3294151356648120293221254337976066366299281810999198800768073487072577972466 96 (chain-addition from primer 32941).

crack_approach: Recover the 5-digit primer (10^5 = 100000 candidates) or use the fact that the chain-addition sequence is fully determined by 5 consecutive digits: hill-climb / SA over the mixed alphabet for each primer guess, scoring with quadgrams. Because the running key digit only shifts within a fixed mixed alphabet, knowing/guessing some primer digits plus the column-transposition keyword (dictionary attack) recovers the rest; CryptoCrack solves even without the primer.

name: Periodic Gromark
algorithm: Like Gromark but the numeric key is PERIODIC. SETUP: (1) The PRIMER length = the keyword length P (this also sets the period). The primer digits are typically the alphabetical-order numbering of the keyword's distinct letters (e.g. KEYWORD -> distinct letters in order of appearance, numbered by alphabetical rank -> primer 3 2 7 6 4 5 1, period 7; TEACHER->TEACHR->631245, period 6). (2) Generate the running key by chain addition (next digit = sum of an adjacent pair mod 10) starting from the P-digit primer, extended to plaintext length, exactly as in Gromark. (3) Build the mixed alphabet from the keyword via columnar transposition as in Gromark. ENCRYPT/DECRYPT: identical substitution rule to Gromark (plaintext index + running-key digit, mod 26, between straight and mixed alphabets), but processed in blocks of size P so that within each period the same keyed-alphabet shift structure repeats; the period P (not 5) is the defining parameter. Encrypt != decrypt.
key_format: A single keyword: its length is the period P, its alphabetical letter-order gives the P-digit primer, and the keyword also builds the mixed alphabet via columnar transposition.

test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Periodic Gromark page (worked example). Running key chain-addition from primer 643125 -> 6431250743757170...

crack_approach: Because the period P is short and embedded, the search space is much smaller than Gromark: try each period length P, recover the P-digit primer (chain-addition seed) and the mixed alphabet by hill-climbing with quadgram fitness; the periodicity lets you split ciphertext into P columns to estimate shifts before solving the keyed alphabet.

name: Ragbaby
algorithm: SETUP: Build a 24-letter keyed alphabet: take a keyword, drop repeated letters, append unused letters A-Z in order, then MERGE J into I and X into W, leaving 24 letters (e.g. FRANKLIN -> FRANKLIBCDEGHMOPQSTUVWYZ). NUMBERING: number the WORDS of the plaintext 1,2,3,...; within each word number the letters consecutively STARTING AT THE WORD NUMBER (word 1: letters 1,2,3,...; word 2: letters 2,3,4,...; etc.). If a position number exceeds 24 it wraps back to 1. ENCRYPT: for each plaintext letter, count FORWARD in the 24-letter keyed alphabet by that letter's position number (wrapping cyclically) to get the ciphertext letter. Word boundaries (spaces) are preserved; hyphenated/apostrophe words count as one word. DECRYPT: count BACKWARD by the same position number. Encrypt != decrypt.
key_format: A single keyword building the 24-letter keyed alphabet (J->I, X->W). The shift schedule is fixed by word/letter position, so word divisions are part of the ciphertext.

test_vectors.source: Wikipedia 'Ragbaby cipher' / dCode.fr canonical example. Word1 RAG shifts 1,2,3; Word2 BABY shifts 2,3,4,5: R+1=S, A+2=P, G+3=M, B+2=T, A+3=H, B+4=D, Y+5=H.

crack_approach: No period; attack via the fixed shift schedule. Word lengths and positions are visible, so guess short words/cribs (the first word's letters shift 1,2,3,... revealing the keyed alphabet head). Hill-climb the 24-letter keyed alphabet with quadgram fitness, or use known-plaintext on common words; the deterministic per-position shift makes a crib on any word recover several alphabet entries directly.

name: Grandpre
algorithm: SETUP: Build an 8x8 grid (ACA size) where each of the 8 ROWS is an 8-letter word AND the 8 letters of the FIRST COLUMN also spell a word; collectively all 26 alphabet letters must appear (so several letters appear multiple times). Number rows 1..8 and columns 1..8 (some implementations/dCode use 1..0 for 10x10; for the 8x8 ACA form use 1..8). ENCRYPT (homophonic): replace each plaintext letter by a two-digit number (row)(column) of SOME cell containing that letter; when a letter occurs in several cells, choose any one (randomly), so a letter has multiple valid codes. Output = stream of two-digit numbers. DECRYPT: read numbers in pairs; (row,column) -> letter at that grid cell. Encrypt != decrypt (encryption is one-to-many; decryption is deterministic).
key_format: Eight 8-letter words (the grid rows) such that the first column also spells a word and all 26 letters are present. No numeric key; the grid IS the key.

test_vectors.plaintext: HAPPINESS IS GOOD HEALTH AND A BAD MEMORY
test_vectors.key: 8x8 grid (rows ADJACENT, NAZARENE, AGGRIEVE, REQUITED, CHATEAUX, HALFBACK, IMPUNITY, CROSSBOW), rows/cols numbered 0-7 in this source
test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Grandpre page (worked example; note this source numbers rows/cols 0-7, e.g. h=(6,1)=61, a=(0,1)=24). dCode.fr uses 1-based numbering for the 10x10 form.

crack_approach: Because it is homophonic with at most 64 distinct codes (8x8) all of which are two-digit pairs, tally code frequencies: the 8x8 has ~64 cells for 26 letters, so high-frequency letters (E,T,A) map to several codes. Use the constraint that each ROW and each COLUMN is a real word (and column 1 is a word) to reconstruct the grid: cluster codes sharing a first digit (same row word) and a second digit (same column word), then solve the crossword-like grid with a dictionary of 8-letter words and n-gram scoring on candidate decryptions.

name: Phillips
algorithm: SETUP: Build a base 5x5 Polybius square (#1) from a keyword (drop duplicates, append unused letters, J merged into I, fill row-wise). Generate 8 squares: from square #1, form #2,#3,#4,#5 by moving ROW 1 down one position at a time (cyclically) while the other rows shift up; then form #6,#7,#8 by moving ROW 2 down one position at a time. (#1 and #5 coincide, #2 and #8 coincide in row-shift variant.) ENCRYPT: process plaintext in groups of 5 letters, using square #1 for letters 1-5, #2 for 6-10, ... #8 for 36-40, then cycle back to #1 (overall PERIOD 40). For each letter, locate it in the CURRENT square and substitute the letter DIAGONALLY DOWN-AND-RIGHT; if the letter is on the BOTTOM row, wrap to the TOP row (same column); if on the RIGHT column, wrap to the LEFT column (same row). DECRYPT: take the letter diagonally UP-AND-LEFT in the corresponding square, wrapping top->bottom and left->right. Encrypt != decrypt. (CryptoCrack offers Row, Column, or Row-Column variants for how the 8 squares are generated.)
key_format: A single keyword (builds the base 5x5 square). Variant selector: Row / Column / Row-Column shift scheme. Fixed period 40.

test_vectors.key: Keyword PATIENCE -> keyed alphabet PATIENCBDFGHKLMOQRSUVWXYZ (J->I); 8 row-shifted squares
test_vectors.ciphertext: DRNDR MAQZL TRSKW OVYAY... (first groups; per-square diagonal-down-right substitution)
test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Phillips page (worked example, keyword PATIENCE).

crack_approach: Period is fixed at 40 (8 squares x 5). Treat as 8 related monoalphabets cyclically, but since all 8 squares derive from ONE 5x5 square, hill-climb / simulated-annealing directly on the single 25-letter keysquare: generate all 8 squares from a candidate, decrypt, and score with quadgram fitness. Slide the 40-period structure to align groups; the diagonal-shift relationship strongly constrains the square so SA converges quickly.

name: Condi
algorithm: Condi = 'CONsecutive DIgraphs'. SETUP: Build a keyed alphabet from a keyword (drop duplicates, append unused letters A-Z in order; 26 letters, J kept separate — full 26-letter alphabet). Number positions 1..26 (CryptoCrack) — note: implementations differ on 0- vs 1-based; be consistent. Choose an INITIAL OFFSET (1..25). ENCRYPT: maintain a current offset. For each plaintext letter P: (1) find P's position p in the keyed alphabet; (2) ciphertext letter = keyed-alphabet letter at position (p + offset) (wrap mod 26); (3) UPDATE: the new offset = p, the position of the PLAINTEXT letter just processed (per ACA/bionspot canonical rule). Repeat. DECRYPT: maintain the same offset; for each ciphertext letter C at position c in the keyed alphabet, plaintext position p = (c - offset) mod 26, recover P, then set offset = p for the next step. Encrypt != decrypt. (AMBIGUITY: CryptoCrack's prose says 'position of this ciphertext letter becomes the new offset', while bionspot/ACA worked examples use the PLAINTEXT letter's position; the plaintext-position rule is the standard ACA implementation.)
key_format: A keyword (26-letter keyed alphabet) + an initial offset 1..25. No fixed period (chaining offset).

test_vectors.key: Keyword CRYPTOGRAM -> keyed alphabet CRYPTOGAMBDEFHIJKLNQSUVWXZ; initial offset 10
test_vectors.source: bionspot.google.site 'CONDI Ciphers' worked example. O(pos6)+10=16->J, then offset=6: N(pos19)+6=25->X, offset=19: T(pos5)+19=24->W, offset=5: H(pos14)+5=19->N, offset=14: E(pos11)+14=25->Z.

crack_approach: Hill-climb / simulated-annealing over the 26-letter keyed alphabet AND the initial offset, scoring decryptions with quadgram fitness. Because the offset chain is deterministic from the keyed alphabet, a correct partial alphabet propagates; cribs on common openings fix the initial offset. Dictionary attack on the keyword reduces the alphabet search.

name: Homophonic
algorithm: ACA Homophonic. SETUP: From a 4-letter keyword (e.g. SLOW), build FOUR numbered 25-letter alphabets (J merged into I). Number 100 cells 01..00 (where 00=100) split into four ranges: alphabet 1 = 01..25, alphabet 2 = 26..50, alphabet 3 = 51..75, alphabet 4 = 76..00. Each alphabet is a straight A..Z (J->I) but offset so the LOWEST number of its range sits under the corresponding keyword letter: with SLOW, number 01 sits under S in alphabet 1, 26 under L in alphabet 2, 51 under O in alphabet 3, 76 under W in alphabet 4; numbering then increases A-order cyclically. Result: each of the 25 letters has exactly FOUR two-digit codes (one per alphabet), arranged in a 4x25 table. ENCRYPT: replace each plaintext letter by ONE of its four numbers, chosen at random (homophonic; flattens frequencies). DECRYPT: look each two-digit number up in the table -> its (unique) letter. Encrypt != decrypt (one-to-many encrypt, deterministic decrypt).
key_format: A 4-letter keyword positioning the four numbered alphabets (4 homophone codes per letter, codes 01..00 = 1..100).

test_vectors.plaintext: HE WHO LAUGHS LAST THINKS SLOWEST (HEWHOLAUGHSLASTTHINKSSLOWEST)
test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Homophonic page (worked example, keyword SLOW). Each letter substituted by one of its 4 numbers chosen at random.

crack_approach: The four codes per letter cluster in four 25-number bands (01-25, 26-50, 51-75, 76-00); reduce by mapping each number n to (n-1) mod 25 — all four homophones of a letter collapse to the SAME residue, turning the cipher into a simple 25-symbol monoalphabetic substitution. Then solve that as an Aristocrat/Patristocrat (frequency + quadgram hill-climb); the keyword falls out from the alphabet offsets.

name: Aristocrat/Patristocrat (keyed alphabet K1-K4)
algorithm: Monoalphabetic substitution. ARISTOCRAT keeps word divisions; PATRISTOCRAT removes them (groups of 5). A keyed alphabet is 'keyword, drop duplicates, append unused letters A-Z in order'. Two alphabets are aligned (PLAINTEXT row over CIPHERTEXT row); the substitution maps plaintext letter -> the ciphertext letter beneath it. KEY TYPES: K1 = keyed PLAINTEXT alphabet, straight (A-Z) ciphertext alphabet. K2 = straight plaintext alphabet, keyed CIPHERTEXT alphabet. K3 = BOTH alphabets keyed with the SAME keyword (and usually offset so no letter maps to itself). K4 = both alphabets keyed with DIFFERENT keywords. ACA RULE: no plaintext letter may encipher to itself; if the natural alignment causes a fixed point, the keyed alphabet is shifted (rotated) until none occur. ENCRYPT: map via plaintext-row -> ciphertext-row. DECRYPT: invert the map. Encrypt != decrypt (it is a fixed permutation, self-inverse only if the permutation happens to be an involution, which is not generally true).
key_format: K1/K2: one keyword (+ an alignment/offset). K3: one keyword used for both alphabets (+ offset). K4: two keywords (one per alphabet, + offset). Optionally a numeric offset/shift to enforce the no-self-map rule.

test_vectors.key: K1, keyword GCARLIN. Keyed PLAINTEXT alphabet gcarlinbdefhjkmopqstuvwxyz aligned over straight CIPHER alphabet shifted: a->Q,b->R,c->S,...,k->A,...
test_vectors.source: CryptoCrack user guide, Aristocrat/Patristocrat page (K1 worked example, keyword GCARLIN). Mapping a->Q b->R c->S d->T e->U f->V g->W h->X i->Y j->Z k->A l->B m->C n->D o->E p->F q->G r->H s->I t->J u->K v->L w->M x->N y->O z->P.

crack_approach: Classic monoalphabetic solve: frequency analysis (single letters, then bigrams/trigrams), pattern words (for Aristocrats with word breaks) against a dictionary, or automated hill-climbing / simulated-annealing on the 26-letter key with quadgram log-probability fitness (works for Patristocrats with no spaces). After recovering the substitution, detect the key type (K1-K4) by testing whether plaintext and/or ciphertext alphabets form keyed-keyword sequences, and recover the keyword(s).

name: Josse
algorithm: Ciphertext-autokey over a KEYED MIXED alphabet (Maj. H. D. Josse, French Army, ~1889; spec recovered by Geraud-Stewart & Naccache, Cryptologia 45(4) 2021). The keyword builds a keyed alphabet which is written row-wise into a table and read back COLUMN-wise; a letter's number is its position in that mixed alphabet. With num()/let() that numbering and its inverse: C_1 = let(-num(P_1) mod n); C_i = let((num(P_i) + num(C_{i-1})) mod n). Decryption is therefore a first difference: P_1 = let(-num(C_1)); P_i = let((num(C_i) - num(C_{i-1})) mod n). Historical Josse omits W (n=25); the 26-letter generalisation is the default (drop=None).
key_format: keyword[/table-width] (width defaults to the count of distinct keyword letters)
reciprocal_note: Encrypt adds the previous CIPHERTEXT number; decrypt subtracts it. Not reciprocal.
crack_approach: Two stages. At the CORRECT numbering the difference sequence D_i = num(C_i) - num(C_{i-1}) equals num(plaintext) exactly, i.e. D is a monoalphabetic image of the plaintext; stage 2 then solves D as an ordinary simple substitution. For stage 1 the practical attack is to sweep KEYWORDS (the numbering is keyword-derived, so the key space is dictionary-sized, not 26!) and score the resulting decode. Lasry (Cryptologia 47(1) 2023) reports a ciphertext-only break from ~75 letters.
notes: MEASURED WARNING on objectives: free-alphabet search over 26! is overfit-undecidable at short lengths (~150 letters). Maximising unigram IoC(D) overfits (a wrong numbering reaches 2.32 vs a true 1.89); sorted-profile matching is too coarse; and even digraph IoC(D) -- which is mono-invariant and an EXCELLENT test (true 4.12 vs random 1.08+-0.23, z+13.3) -- is beaten by free search (9.42). Use it to TEST a candidate numbering, never to search for one; search the keyword space instead.

name: Polybius
algorithm: A keyed mixed 5x5 square (25-letter alphabet, J merged into I). Each plaintext letter is replaced by its 1-indexed (row)(column) coordinate pair, row first. ENCRYPT: letter -> two digits in 1..5. DECRYPT: inverse lookup. No fractionation, transposition or additive is applied, so the cipher is a pure monoalphabetic substitution written in a two-digit alphabet.
key_format: A keyword for the mixed square; an empty key gives the standard A-Z (J->I) square.

test_vectors.source: Wikipedia 'Polybius square' / dCode.fr Polybius cipher — ZEBRAS square places D at row 2, column 3
Standard A-Z (J->I) square: A is row 1, column 1
Standard A-Z (J->I) square: Z is row 5, column 5

crack_approach: Solve outright rather than searching keywords. Each distinct coordinate pair stands for exactly one plaintext letter, so relabel the (row,col) pairs as proxy symbols and the problem IS the monoalphabetic substitution problem — hand it to a quadgram hill-climbing substitution solver. The square is then read off the solved map; cells whose pair never occurs in the ciphertext are unconstrained and stay unknown.
notes: Ciphertext alphabet is restricted to the digits 1-5, which rules the cipher out immediately for any other input.

name: Collon
algorithm: A keyed mixed 5x5 square (J->I) plus a group size N. Split the plaintext into groups of N. For each group emit the ROW LABEL of every letter, then the COLUMN LABEL of every letter. The row label of row r is the letter at (r,0); the column label of column c is the letter at (4,c). Ciphertext is therefore twice the plaintext length and written in letters, not digits. DECRYPT: split each 2N-character block into N row labels and N column labels, pair them positionally, and read the square at the intersection of the row containing L1 and the column containing L2 (any letter identifies its row or column, not only the canonical label). A short final group of m letters is emitted as 2m characters.
key_format: 'KEYWORD/N' — square keyword and group size; an empty keyword gives the standard square.

test_vectors.source: dCode.fr Collon cipher — standard square, N=2: D is row A column Y, C is row A column X, so rows AA then columns YX
dCode.fr Collon cipher — N=3, rows AKK and columns XZV pair to AX, KZ, KV

crack_approach: Do NOT anneal the 25-cell square (measured 0/5). Only five letters can appear in a row position and five in a column position, so the ciphertext alphabet is at most 10 and each (row label, column label) pair maps to exactly one plaintext letter — a monoalphabetic substitution over at most 25 pair-symbols, solved directly. The group size falls out of the same constraint: at the true N the row half and column half of each block each draw on only five letters, and a wrong N mixes them. The square is recovered only up to a permutation of rows and of columns, which costs nothing because a label travels with its row, so every consistent ordering decodes identically.
notes: The 10-letter ciphertext alphabet is the cipher's signature and its undoing.

name: Ubchi
algorithm: Double columnar transposition REUSING one permutation key. (1) Columnar-transpose the plaintext under the keyword. (2) Append n null letters to the intermediate result. (3) Columnar-transpose that under the SAME keyword. DECRYPT: undo the outer transposition, drop the n trailing nulls, undo the inner one. Used by the German army in WWI.
key_format: 'KEYWORD' or 'KEYWORD/NULLS' (e.g. UBER/1); the permutation may also be given as an explicit 0-based read order such as '1,2,3,0/1'. NULLS defaults to 0.

test_vectors.source: dCode.fr Ubchi cipher — UBER sorts to B,E,R,U giving read order 1,2,3,0; SECRET -> ETCRSE, padded to ETCRSEX, -> TECXRES

crack_approach: The key reuse is the weakness. A general double transposition needs two independent permutations (width 6 alone is 518400 pairs); reusing one collapses the search to w! per width, and widths 2..8 together are under 46000 orders — enumerable outright. Try each order against every plausible null count, since the count shifts the intermediate length and a wrong count decodes to garbage. Rank by n-gram fitness.
notes: Distinguish from a general double transposition, which uses two different keys and is not enumerable this way.

name: Chaocipher
algorithm: Two 26-letter alphabets, LEFT (ciphertext) and RIGHT (plaintext), both permuted after EVERY letter. To encipher: find the plaintext letter at index i of RIGHT; the ciphertext letter is LEFT[i]. Then permute LEFT — rotate so LEFT[i] sits at position 0 (zenith), remove the letter now at position 1 and re-insert it at position 13 (nadir), sliding positions 2..13 down one. Then permute RIGHT — rotate so RIGHT[i] sits at position 0, rotate one place further, remove the letter at position 2 and re-insert it at position 13. DECRYPT: find the ciphertext letter in LEFT, read RIGHT at the same index; the permutation step is identical so both directions stay in lockstep. Invented by John F. Byrne in 1918; algorithm disclosed 2010.
key_format: 'LEFT/RIGHT' — two 26-letter permutations of A-Z.

test_vectors.source: Moshe Rubin, 'Chaocipher Revealed: The Algorithm' (2010), Exhibit 1 of the Byrne papers

crack_approach: No keyless attack exists and none should be attempted. The keyspace is two independent 26-letter permutations (~2^177) and it cannot be climbed: the alphabets permute after each letter, so one wrong cell corrupts the ENTIRE remaining decrypt rather than one position of it, and the n-gram score of a nearly correct key is indistinguishable from that of a random one — there is no gradient. Published cryptanalysis (Deavours and Kruh) is a known-plaintext attack needing roughly 50-100 aligned characters.
notes: A repeated plaintext block does NOT give a repeated ciphertext block; no period is recoverable by any statistic.

name: M-94 (Jefferson cylinder)
algorithm: Twenty-five disks on a spindle, each carrying the 26 letters in its own scrambled order. The ORDER of the disks is the key. The operator turns each disk until the plaintext letters read across one row (the generatrix), then copies off any other row; the offset between the two rows is the second half of the key. For disk d with alphabet A_d and plaintext letter p at position j: ciphertext = A_d[(A_d.index(p) + offset) % 26]. Messages longer than the disk count wrap, so positions j and j+width pass through the same disk. M-138 is the same machine built from sliding strips — a subset of a larger strip set in a chosen order — modelled by giving a shorter disk order. Fielded by the US Army 1922-1943.
key_format: 'ORDER/OFFSET' — comma-separated 1-based disk numbers and a row offset 1..25 (offset 0 is the identity). Any number of disks from 2 to 25.

test_vectors.source: Wikipedia 'M-94 (cipher machine)' documents that the 17th disc begins 'ARMY OF THE US'; full 25-disk table from the CrypTool 2 CylinderCipher Cylinders_M94.txt

crack_approach: The order is a permutation of 25 disks (15511210043330985984000000 arrangements), so no brute force. But positions j and j+width share a disk, so the ciphertext splits into width independent columns and, for a fixed offset, each column decrypts under each disk in exactly one way. 'Which disk sits in which position' is therefore a maximum-weight bipartite ASSIGNMENT, solved exactly by Hungarian with per-cell weights from English monogram log-likelihood. Follow it with a pairwise-swap hill climb on the quadgram score of the whole reconstructed plaintext — swapping preserves the permutation, and that step supplies the cross-column context no per-column score can see. Recovers a full 25-disk order from ~228 letters (9 per column).
notes: Each disk is identified by the letter following A on it, from 'B 1' to 'Z 25'.

name: Enigma (M3)
algorithm: Three rotors chosen from I-VIII, a reflector (UKW-B or UKW-C), ring settings and a plugboard. A key press steps the rotors, then the current runs plugboard -> right rotor -> middle -> left -> reflector -> left -> middle -> right -> plugboard. Stepping includes the double-step anomaly: the middle rotor advances both when the right rotor passes its notch and, on the very next press, together with the left rotor when the middle rotor is itself on its notch. A rotor at position p with ring setting r applies shift = p - r, so forward(c) = (wiring[(c+shift)%26] - shift)%26 and backward(c) = (inverse[(c+shift)%26] - shift)%26. Turnover is read off the window letter, so a rotor is at its notch when its POSITION equals the notch letter, independent of the ring. Rotor notches: I=Q, II=E, III=V, IV=J, V=Z, VI/VII/VIII=Z and M.
key_format: 'ROTORS/REFLECTOR/RINGS/POSITIONS[/PLUGBOARD]' — e.g. 'I II III/B/AAA/AAA/AB CD EF'. Rotors listed left to right; rings and positions three letters each; plugboard is space-separated letter pairs.

test_vectors.source: Standard Enigma I verification vector (rotors I II III, reflector B, rings AAA, positions AAA, no plugboard)
Canonical 26-letter Enigma I output, exercising the first turnover cycle and the double-step anomaly

crack_approach: Gillogly's three phases. (1) Sweep every rotor order and all 17576 start positions with rings AAA and an empty plugboard, ranking by the decrypt's index of coincidence — this works despite wrong rings and plugboard because IoC is invariant under the plugboard (a fixed substitution) and a wrong ring only mis-times a turnover. IoC is a whole-message statistic: on a 350-letter plant the true setting ranks 1070th when only 120 letters are scored and 1st at full length, so do not truncate the probe. (2) Sweep the ring settings on the n-gram score, which does see the turnover error; a ring and its rotor position shift together, so the position must follow the ring. (3) Grow the plugboard greedily — try all 325 unused letter pairs, keep the one that most improves the n-gram score, repeat up to ten leads. When the rotor order AND a non-trivial ring setting are both unknown, the right-hand ring must also be swept in phase 1 (26x cost): a measured plant put the true setting 128720th of 1054560 by IoC otherwise.
notes: The reflector makes the machine reciprocal (encrypt == decrypt) and guarantees no letter ever encrypts to itself — the two facts every attack rests on. Reflectors must be involutions.
